title: "Scripts"

```{term}
#| include: false
rush run -o mtcars.csv 'mtcars'
```

Every `rush` command writes a small R script and runs it. With `--dry-run`
(`-n`), `rush` prints that script instead, so you can save it, edit it, and run
it again later.

## Saving a script

The script that `--dry-run` prints is a complete, self-contained
[`ir`](https://r-lib.github.io/ir/) script. Redirect it to a file:

```{term}
rush run --dry-run 'dplyr::filter(df, hp > 200)' mtcars.csv > analysis.R
cat analysis.R
```

The `#|` frontmatter at the top declares the packages the script needs. That
includes `rush` itself, which the script refers to on GitHub
(`github::jeroenjanssens/rush`), pinned to the commit or release that
generated it, so the script keeps working when `rush` changes.

## Which packages a script needs

`rush` lists every package that the script needs in the `#|` header, so that
`ir` can install them. To see the list, print the script with `--dry-run` and
keep only the header with `grep`. A script always needs `rush` and a few
packages that `rush` itself uses:

```{term}
rush run -n '6 * 7' | grep '^#|'
```

Other packages are added for what the script does. Reading a file adds its
reader, and janitor, which cleans the column names:

```{term}
rush run -n 'nrow(df)' mtcars.parquet | grep '^#|'
```

Writing a file adds its writer, here writexl for Excel:

```{term}
rush run -n -o cars.xlsx 'head(df)' mtcars.csv | grep '^#|'
```

`--library` (`-l`) adds the packages you name, and `--tidyverse` (`-t`) adds
the tidyverse and glue:

```{term}
rush run -n -l lubridate 'today()' | grep '^#|'
```

Packages that your R code calls with `pkg::` are added too, so you don't need
`-l` for them:

```{term}
rush run -n 'stringr::str_to_title("hello")' | grep '^#|'
```

And so are packages that your code loads with `library()`:

```{term}
rush run -n 'library(glue); glue("6 * 7 = {6 * 7}")' | grep '^#|'
```

Plots add ggplot2 and the packages that draw in the terminal. Packages in the
aesthetics and in `--pre` and `--post` are added as well, here forcats:

```{term}
rush plot -n -x 'forcats::fct_infreq(class)' mpg.csv | grep '^#|'
```

In short:

| A package is added for | Example |
|------------------------|---------|
| Reading a file | `mtcars.parquet` adds nanoparquet |
| Writing a file | `-o cars.xlsx` adds writexl, `-o plot.svg` adds svglite |
| `--library` (`-l`) | `-l lubridate` adds lubridate |
| `--tidyverse` (`-t`) | adds tidyverse and glue |
| `pkg::` in R code | `stringr::str_to_title()` adds stringr |
| `library()` in R code | `library(glue)` adds glue |
| A plot | ggplot2, and devoutansi for the terminal |

Packages that come with R, such as stats and utils, are never listed, because
they are always installed.

## Running a script

Run it with `ir run`. `ir` installs any missing packages, so the script needs
nothing but `ir` on the machine that runs it:

```{term}
ir run analysis.R
```

The `#!/usr/bin/env -S ir run` line at the top also makes the file
executable (`chmod +x analysis.R && ./analysis.R`). This is handy for
tweaking: dump a `rush` one-liner to a file, edit the generated R to do
something `rush` doesn't express directly, and run it later.

## Scripts without rush

The script above calls helper functions from `rush`, such as `rush::read()`,
which keeps it short. Add `--no-rush` (`-R`) for a script with all of that
code inlined, which doesn't need `rush` at all:

```{term}
rush run -n -R 'dplyr::filter(df, hp > 200)' mtcars.csv > standalone.R
wc -l analysis.R standalone.R
```

The script is longer, but it only uses common packages such as readr, and it
runs the same way:

```{term}
ir run standalone.R
```

## Formatting with air

If the [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) formatter is on your `PATH`,
`rush` runs the `--dry-run` output through it, so the printed script is neatly
formatted and ready to save. This affects only what `--dry-run` shows; the
script that actually runs is never reformatted.

## Running without `ir`

By default `rush` runs each script with `ir`, which installs the packages
declared in the frontmatter when needed. If you would rather use the packages
already installed in your R library (for speed, to work offline, or in an
environment where dependencies are pinned), pass `--no-ir` (`-I`), and `rush`
runs the script with plain `Rscript` instead:

```{term}
rush run --no-ir '6 * 7'
```

Nothing is installed in this mode, so every package the script needs must
already be present. Because nothing reads the `#|` frontmatter, `rush` leaves
it out, and the script starts with an `Rscript` shebang instead. You can see
this when you combine `--no-ir` with `--dry-run`:

```{term}
rush run -n -I 'dplyr::filter(df, hp > 200)' mtcars.csv > installed.R
cat installed.R
```

Run it with `Rscript installed.R`, or make it executable
(`chmod +x installed.R && ./installed.R`), and it uses your installed
packages, just like `rush --no-ir` does. For a script that `ir` can run
anywhere, print it again without `--no-ir`.

## A plain R script

Combine `--dry-run`, `--no-ir`, and `--no-rush` for a plain R script that
needs neither `rush` nor `ir`, only `Rscript` and the packages it uses. Here
is the whole script for the same filter as above. It's long, because it
contains all the code that `rush` uses to read the file and write the result:

```{term}
rush run -n -I -R 'dplyr::filter(df, hp > 200)' mtcars.csv
```

```{term}
#| include: false
rm -f mtcars.csv analysis.R standalone.R installed.R
```
